subtopics.title: Matter Is Particles — and Here Is the Evidence

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the statements of the Kinetic Molecular Theory?
options: All matter is made of particles
The particles are in constant, random motion
The particles themselves expand when heated
There are forces of attraction between the particles

questions.question: Smoke particles viewed under a microscope jerk along jagged, unpredictable paths. This is called Brownian motion, and it is evidence that:
options: smoke is a liquid
invisible air particles exist and are permanently in motion, bombarding the specks unevenly
the microscope lens is vibrating
smoke particles repel one another

questions.question: Temperature is best defined as:
options: the total energy contained in a substance
the energy transferred because of a temperature difference
the number of particles in a substance
a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles

questions.question: Why does diffusion happen faster in a gas than in a liquid?
options: Gas particles move faster and meet less obstruction
Gas particles are larger
Gases have stronger forces of attraction
Liquids have no particle motion at all

subtopics.title: Solid, Liquid and Gas in the Kinetic Molecular Theory

questions.question: In a solid, the particles:
options: move rapidly in straight lines between collisions
slide past one another in an irregular arrangement
vibrate about fixed positions in a regular lattice
are far apart with negligible forces between them

questions.question: A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape because:
options: its particles are far apart with no forces between them
its particles stay close together but can slide past one another
its particles are locked in a lattice
its particles have no kinetic energy

questions.question: Why is a gas easy to compress while a solid is not?
options: Gas particles are softer than solid particles
Gas particles attract each other strongly
Gases are always hotter than solids
Most of a gas's volume is empty space between widely separated particles, while a solid has almost no space between its particles

questions.question: The state a substance occupies is decided by:
options: the contest between the particles' kinetic energy and the forces of attraction between them
the size of the particles alone
the number of particles present
the shape of the container

subtopics.title: The Six Changes of State and the Energy They Need

questions.question: Frost forming on grass on a cold Highveld night, with water vapour becoming ice without ever being liquid, is:
options: sublimation
condensation
deposition
freezing

questions.question: Which set contains ONLY endothermic changes of state?
options: Freezing, condensation, deposition
Melting, evaporation, sublimation
Melting, condensation, deposition
Freezing, evaporation, sublimation

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes evaporation from boiling?
options: Evaporation happens only at the boiling point; boiling happens at any temperature
Both happen only at the boiling point, but boiling is faster
Evaporation occurs at any temperature and only at the surface; boiling occurs at the boiling point and throughout the liquid
Evaporation happens throughout the liquid; boiling happens only at the surface

questions.question: Water boils at about 95 °C on the Highveld but at about 100 °C at the coast because:
options: atmospheric pressure is lower at altitude, so the vapour pressure matches it at a lower temperature
Highveld water is less pure
the boiling point of water is not a fixed property of the substance at all pressures anywhere
the air is colder inland

subtopics.title: Reading a Heating Curve — Why the Temperature Stops Rising

questions.question: Ice is heated steadily from −20 °C. Why does the temperature stay at 0 °C for a period even though heating continues?
options: The heater stops supplying energy during melting
The thermometer cannot read a mixture
The energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles, raising potential energy rather than kinetic energy
The ice reflects the heat while it melts

questions.question: On a heating curve for water, the plateau at 100 °C is markedly longer than the plateau at 0 °C because:
options: the thermometer responds more slowly at higher temperatures
separating liquid particles completely into a gas takes far more energy than loosening a lattice into a liquid
the water loses mass while boiling
boiling happens more slowly at altitude

questions.question: Which states are present at a point exactly on the 0 °C plateau of the heating curve?
options: Solid only
Liquid only
Liquid and gas together
Solid and liquid together

questions.question: A temperature of 100 °C expressed in kelvin is:

subtopics.title: The Assembly, the Crowd and the Open Field

questions.question: In the assembly picture, learners standing in neat rows and fidgeting on the spot represent:
options: a gas
a liquid
a solid
a vacuum

questions.question: The crowd flooding a corridor — still packed but sliding past one another and taking the corridor's shape — is a picture of:
options: a liquid, which keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container
a gas, which fills any space it is given
a solid changing to a gas directly
particles that have stopped moving

questions.question: In the tug-of-war picture, what happens when the jiggling wins outright over the pull between particles?
options: The particles lock into rows — a solid
The particles slide but stay together — a liquid
The particles stop moving altogether
The particles scatter and fill the space — a gas

subtopics.title: Why the Pot Sticks at One Hundred

questions.question: The stove is on full but the thermometer in the pot stays at 100 °C. The energy is:
options: being reflected back out of the pot
breaking the grips between water particles and setting them free, not making them faster
no longer entering the water
being turned into extra water

questions.question: In the 'paying off a debt' picture, who is the debt collector?
options: The thermometer
The kinetic energy of the particles
The forces of attraction holding the particles together
The container walls

questions.question: Ice taken from a deep freeze at −20 °C and heated steadily will:
options: warm to 0 °C, stick at 0 °C as a slush until the last ice is gone, then warm towards 100 °C
melt gradually the whole way from −20 °C to 100 °C
jump straight to 100 °C
stay at −20 °C until it has all melted

questions.question: Why is a steam burn worse than a burn from water at the same 100 °C?
options: Steam is at a higher temperature than boiling water
Steam particles are bigger
Steam contains extra chemicals
As it condenses on your skin, the steam gives back all the separation energy it absorbed when it boiled

subtopics.title: Six Words for Changing, and the Traps That Cost Marks

questions.question: Dry ice smoking away without ever making a puddle is an example of:
options: sublimation — solid straight to gas
deposition — gas straight to solid
condensation
melting followed by rapid evaporation

questions.question: The one-question sort for energy direction is 'am I loosening the grip or tightening it?'. Tightening the grip means:
options: energy must be supplied
energy is released
the temperature must rise
the substance becomes a gas

questions.question: Which sentence would LOSE marks in an exam?
options: During melting the energy breaks the forces between the particles
During melting the potential energy of the particles increases
During melting no energy is going into the substance because the temperature is constant
During melting solid and liquid are present together

questions.question: A pot of boiling water and a swimming pool heated to boiling point differ in that:
options: the pot is at a higher temperature
the pool's particles jiggle harder
they are at the same temperature, but the pool holds vastly more heat energy
the pool would boil at a lower temperature
